# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, particularly those valuing data ownership and customization. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to host their data on their servers, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, as teams can add their own servers to support growth.
* Feature difference: Element supports end-to-end encryption, while Slack does not.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with other tools
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Customizable notifications
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* End-to-end encryption support
* Highly customizable
* Scalable
* Open-source
* Limited user support resources
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited integration with other tools
* Mobile app support is improving but still limited

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that value ease of use and a wide range of integrations with other tools. It's suitable for teams of all sizes, from small startups to large enterprises. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for teams that value data ownership and customization. It's particularly suitable for teams with technical expertise and a need for end-to-end encryption.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations with other tools.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some features and polish. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's mobile app support is still limited, which may be a concern for teams with many mobile users. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching if you have the technical expertise to set it up and maintain it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need many integrations with other tools
* Technical teams that value data ownership and customization
* Teams that require end-to-end encryption
* Teams with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user costs
* Teams with high security requirements that need more control over their data

## FAQ
### Is Element free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted.
### Can I use Element with my existing Slack integrations?
Some integrations may work with Element, but many will not, as Element has its own API and integration system.
### How difficult is it to set up Element?
Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain than Slack, but it's still possible for non-technical teams to use with some support.
### Can I use Element on my mobile device?
Yes, Element has mobile apps for Android and iOS, but they are still limited in terms of features and functionality.
### Is Element suitable for large enterprises?
Not yet, as Element still lacks some features and polish, and may not be scalable enough for very large teams.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as messaging, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those valuing data ownership and customization. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch is to gain more control over data and costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack is generally easier to set up, with a more streamlined onboarding process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility.
* Integration difference: Mattermost has a more extensive range of customization options and integrations with other tools, particularly for development teams, through its use of webhooks and APIs.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with other tools
* Good mobile apps
* Strong support for video and voice calls
* Limited customization options
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosted option for data control and customization
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Good for development teams with existing infrastructure
* Can be complex to set up and manage
* Limited support for video and voice calls

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, particularly those without extensive technical expertise. It's suitable for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, cloud-based communication platform. On the other hand, Mattermost is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data and customization options. It's particularly well-suited for development teams that already have existing infrastructure and technical expertise.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool, such as the Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which supports JSON format.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance with the necessary integrations and customizations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Mattermost is production-ready for most users, offering a reliable and feature-rich platform for team collaboration. However, one specific technical limitation to consider is its limited support for video and voice calls, which may not be suitable for all teams. Overall, we recommend switching to Mattermost for teams that value data ownership and customization, particularly those with existing technical infrastructure.

Mattermost's self-hosted option provides a high degree of control and flexibility, making it an attractive choice for teams that require customization. However, this also means that teams will need to have the necessary technical expertise to set up and manage their own server.

For teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations, Slack may still be the better choice. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, Mattermost is definitely worth considering.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need video and voice calls
* Development teams with existing infrastructure and technical expertise
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that need customization options and data control
* Teams that require self-hosting for security or compliance reasons
* Teams that don't need a wide range of integrations with other tools

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, which allows teams to host their own servers and have full control over their data.

### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free to use, with a self-hosted option that has no per-user costs. However, teams will need to pay for their own server costs.

### Can I import my Slack data into Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost supports importing data from Slack, using the Slack API or a third-party tool.

### Does Mattermost support video and voice calls?
Mattermost has limited support for video and voice calls, which may not be suitable for all teams.

### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Yes, Mattermost can be suitable for small teams, particularly those that value data ownership and customization.

# Slack vs Zulip (2026)

* Data ownership: Zulip allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Zulip requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Zulip is designed to scale horizontally, making it more suitable for large teams, while Slack's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration with GitHub: Slack has native integration with GitHub, while Zulip requires a third-party plugin.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Zulip |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Native integration with many third-party services
* Good mobile app support
* Large user community
* Limited control over data
### Zulip
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Highly customizable
* Scalable architecture
* Free and open-source
* Steeper learning curve due to more complex features

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't mind paying a premium for a proprietary solution. It's also a good fit for teams that already use many third-party services that integrate with Slack. Zulip, on the other hand, is a better choice for large teams or organizations that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own servers.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Zulip server and configure it to your needs.
3. Use the Zulip import tool to import your Slack data into Zulip.
4. Test your Zulip setup to ensure everything is working as expected.
5. Update your team's workflows and documentation to reflect the switch to Zulip.

## Our Take
Zulip is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the polish and ease of use that Slack offers. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Zulip's mobile app support is still in development, and may not be as robust as Slack's. However, for teams that prioritize data control and customization, Zulip is a clear winner, and we recommend switching to Zulip if you have a large team and are willing to invest in setting up and maintaining your own servers.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) that require full control over their data
* Teams that don't need native integration with GitHub
* Organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements
* Teams that are already familiar with self-hosted solutions
* Companies with limited budgets that can't afford Slack's per-user costs

## FAQ
### Can I use Zulip for free?
Yes, Zulip is free and open-source, and you can self-host it on your own servers.

### Can I import my Slack data into Zulip?
Yes, Zulip offers an import tool that can import your Slack data.
### Is Zulip available as a cloud-hosted solution?

### Can I use Zulip on my mobile device?
Yes, but the mobile app is still in development and may not be as robust as Slack's.

# Discord vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Discord and Element are communication platforms designed for communities and teams. This comparison is useful for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with a core use case of secure and customizable team communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce dependence on third-party services.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Discord offers a free plan with limitations, while Element is free and self-hosted, with costs limited to server maintenance.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, while Discord's terms of service grant the company access to user data.
* Setup complexity: Discord is generally easier to set up, with a more user-friendly interface, while Element requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Element is highly scalable, with the ability to support large communities and teams, while Discord's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Feature difference: Element offers end-to-end encryption by default, while Discord only offers encryption for direct messages.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $4.99/month (billed annually) | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Discord:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large user base and community
* Good for gaming and social communities
* Offers screen sharing and video conferencing
* Limited control over data and customization
**Element:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Highly customizable and secure
* End-to-end encryption by default
* Scalable and suitable for large teams
* Requires technical expertise to set up and maintain

## When to Choose Each
Discord is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams, gaming communities, and social groups that prioritize ease of use and a large user base. Element, on the other hand, is suitable for large teams, organizations, and communities that require high levels of customization, security, and control over their data.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Discord data using the Discord export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your chat history and other data.
2. Set up an Element server and create a new account.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Discord data, which supports JSON files.
4. Configure your Element server and customize your settings as needed.
5. Invite your team members to join your new Element server.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and maintain. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's integration with other services is still limited compared to Discord. However, for teams and organizations that require high levels of customization and security, Element is a good choice, and we recommend switching if you have the technical expertise and resources to support it.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that require high levels of security and customization
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that need more control over their data and communication
* Large teams (50-200 users) that require scalable and customizable communication solutions
* Organizations that prioritize data ownership and security
* Communities that need end-to-end encryption and secure communication

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, with costs limited to server maintenance.
### Is Element compatible with Discord?
No, Element and Discord are two separate platforms with different architectures and features.
### Can I import my Discord data into Element?
Yes, Element provides an import tool that supports JSON files exported from Discord.
### Is Element suitable for gaming communities?
No, Element is not yet suitable for gaming communities, as it lacks some of the features and integrations that Discord offers.
### Can I self-host Element on my own server?
Yes, Element can be self-hosted on your own server, giving you full control over your data and customization.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Obsidian is a free, self-hosted alternative to Notion. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control platforms that help developers manage their codebases. This comparison is beneficial for developers, development teams, and organizations looking to switch from one platform to the other, with the core use case being collaborative software development. The key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data, reduce costs, or take advantage of specific features.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free plans with limited features, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option with more features.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows users to self-host their repositories, giving them full control over their data, while GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitLab requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, while GitHub is generally easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option allows for more flexibility in terms of customizing the infrastructure.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers a built-in Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) tool, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations for CI/CD.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**GitHub:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers free plans with limited features
* Limited control over data and customization options
**GitLab:**
* Offers more features, including CI/CD and project management tools
* Self-hosted option gives users full control over their data
* More customizable than GitHub
* Can be more complex to set up and manage
* Limited support for some third-party integrations

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require a high level of customization. It's also a good option for teams that are already invested in the GitHub ecosystem and don't want to switch to a new platform. GitLab, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations that require more control over their data and want to take advantage of advanced features like CI/CD. It's also a good option for teams that want to self-host their repositories and have more customization options.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Create a new repository on GitLab and navigate to the import page.
3. Select "GitHub" as the import source and follow the prompts to authenticate with your GitHub account.
4. Choose the repository you want to import and select the branches you want to transfer.
5. Use the GitLab import tool to transfer your repository data.

---

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and a self-hosted option that gives users full control over their data. However, one technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's self-hosted option requires more technical expertise to set up and manage, which can be a barrier for smaller teams or those without dedicated IT staff. We recommend switching to GitLab if you're a larger team or organization that requires more control over your data and wants to take advantage of advanced features like CI/CD.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (50+ users) that require more control over their data and want to take advantage of advanced features like CI/CD.
* Organizations that prioritize data security and want to self-host their repositories.
* Development teams that require more customization options and are willing to invest time in setting up and managing their own infrastructure.
* Teams that don't require tight integration with other GitHub tools and are looking for a more cost-effective solution.
* Open-source projects that want to take advantage of GitLab's free self-hosted option and advanced features.

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free plan with limited features for its cloud-based platform.
### Can I self-host my GitHub repository?
No, GitHub does not offer a self-hosted option.
### Is GitLab compatible with GitHub?
Yes, GitLab is compatible with GitHub, and you can import your GitHub repository into GitLab using the import tool.
### Does GitLab offer CI/CD tools?
Yes, GitLab offers a built-in CI/CD tool that allows you to automate your testing and deployment pipeline.
### Can I use GitLab with my existing GitHub workflow?
Yes, GitLab is designed to be compatible with existing GitHub workflows, and you can use many of the same tools and integrations with GitLab.

# GitHub vs Gitea

## Overview

The world largest code hosting and collaboration platform. Owned by Microsoft since 2018. is a popular proprietary tool in the developer-tools space. Gitea is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub costs Free / $7-$21/user; Gitea is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: GitHub is Proprietary; Gitea is MIT
- **Data ownership**: Gitea can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Gitea eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Gitea has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Gitea

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [go-gitea/gitea](https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea) * ~44k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Gitea if:** Gitea is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from GitHub in its standard export format, review Gitea import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Gitea is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Gitea instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted Gitea will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Gitea free to use?
Yes. Gitea is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to Gitea?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the Gitea import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Gitea get regular updates?
Yes. Gitea has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Gitea without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Gitea development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [Gitea](https://gitea.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Gitea is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by designers, developers, and product teams to create user interfaces, websites, and applications. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals looking to switch from Figma to Penpot, possibly due to the core use case of needing a free or self-hosted solution. The key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their design data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma has a per-user pricing model, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Figma stores design data on its proprietary servers, whereas Penpot allows users to self-host and maintain full control over their data.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more streamlined setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and projects, while Penpot's scalability is still being developed and tested.
* Feature difference: Figma has a more comprehensive set of features, including advanced prototyping and collaboration tools, while Penpot has a more limited feature set, but is rapidly developing and adding new features.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ Comprehensive set of features
	+ Streamlined setup process
	+ Scalable and reliable infrastructure
	+ Large community and ecosystem
	+ Advanced collaboration and prototyping tools
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over design data
	+ Proprietary software
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full data control
	+ Rapidly developing and improving
	+ Growing community and ecosystem
	+ Customizable and extensible
* Cons:
	+ Limited feature set compared to Figma
	+ More complex setup process, especially for self-hosting
	+ Still developing and testing scalability
	+ Limited support and resources compared to Figma
	+ May require more technical expertise

## When to Choose Each
Figma is a better choice for large teams or enterprises that require a comprehensive set of features, advanced collaboration and prototyping tools, and a scalable and reliable infrastructure. It is also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the Figma ecosystem and have a large library of design files. On the other hand, Penpot is a better choice for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who are looking for a free or self-hosted solution, and are willing to trade off some features and complexity for more control over their design data.

Penpot is also a good choice for teams that are looking for a customizable and extensible solution, and are willing to contribute to the development and growth of the Penpot community. Additionally, teams that are already familiar with open-source software and have the technical expertise to set up and configure Penpot may find it to be a good fit.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma design files in the Figma API JSON format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to import your Figma design files into Penpot.
3. Review and update your design files to ensure compatibility with Penpot's feature set and formatting.
4. Set up and configure your Penpot instance, including self-hosting if desired.
5. Test and verify that your design files and workflows are functioning as expected in Penpot.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users, as it is still developing and testing its features and scalability. However, it shows great promise and potential for teams and individuals looking for a free or self-hosted solution. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Penpot's support for advanced prototyping and collaboration tools is still limited compared to Figma.

For teams and individuals who are looking for a free or self-hosted solution and are willing to trade off some features and complexity, Penpot may be a good choice. However, for large teams or enterprises that require a comprehensive set of features and advanced collaboration and prototyping tools, Figma may still be the better choice. We recommend that teams and individuals carefully evaluate their needs and requirements before switching to Penpot.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need advanced collaboration and prototyping tools
* Individuals or solo designers who are looking for a free solution
* Teams that are already familiar with open-source software and have the technical expertise to set up and configure Penpot
* Teams that require self-hosting and full control over their design data
* Teams that are looking for a customizable and extensible solution and are willing to contribute to the development and growth of the Penpot community

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for large teams or enterprises?
No, Penpot is still developing and testing its scalability, and may not be suitable for large teams or enterprises. However, it is rapidly improving and may be a good choice in the future.
### Is Penpot compatible with Figma design files?
Yes, Penpot has an import tool that allows you to import Figma design files in the Figma API JSON format.
### Can I self-host Penpot?
Yes, Penpot allows self-hosting, which gives you full control over your design data and allows you to customize and extend the software to meet your needs.
### Is Penpot free?
Yes, Penpot is free and open-source, with no per-user costs or licensing fees.
### Can I use Penpot for advanced prototyping and collaboration?
Not yet, Penpot's support for advanced prototyping and collaboration tools is still limited compared to Figma. However, it is rapidly developing and improving.
